aboutYou.name: Peig Hannigan
aboutYou.appearance: a sharp-eyed woman with a satchel of letters
aboutYou.personality: Peig keeps the Letter Office and watches the village road. She is sharp-witted and plain-spoken, kind beneath the wit, and knows who has had news from beyond the parish. She keeps private letters private.

knows: Peig keeps the Letter Office and knows who has received news from beyond the parish.
Mícheál and Róisín Connolly share the cottage west of the village.
backstory: She grew up on a small farm by the shore of Lough Ree and learned her letters from a hedge-school master.
Her husband died in the fever of 1818; they had no children, and she has kept the Letter Office alone since.
She has read too many letters from America announcing deaths to think well of the passage.
She hopes to see the Letter Office made a proper post office, with the post coming by mail-car and not by a boy on a tired horse.

commonKnowledge.text: Kilteevan parish, a few miles south-east of Roscommon town, County Roscommon, in the province of Connacht, spring 1820. The parish runs east to Lough Ree and the Shannon, with much bog.

Roscommon town, with its Saturday corn market, its fairs (Whit-Monday and 15 December), the assizes and the new county gaol. Athlone about fifteen miles south; Strokestown to the north-east; Boyle to the north; Dublin as a far place few have seen. America as where people go and seldom come back from.

Ireland part of the United Kingdom since the Act of Union took effect in 1801, ruled from London through the Lord Lieutenant and Dublin Castle. The old King George III died this January; George IV is king, not yet crowned. Catholics with enough property can vote but cannot sit in Parliament or hold high office; emancipation is talked of, not won.

Most people rent from a landlord, usually through an agent or middleman; rent day and the fear of eviction. Tithes to the Established Church, whatever your own faith, collected by the proctor. Conacre, the potato as the poor family's food, oats and cattle for the rent. Prices in Irish shillings and pence.
The failed harvest of 1816, the hunger of 1817, and the fever that ran through the country from then until last year.
The priest and Mass; the Church of Ireland rector and his tithes; holy wells and pattern days; wakes; the feast days of the year; the good people, spoken of carefully.
Irish and English both spoken, Irish most at home and among the old; hedge schools; many cannot read.
Walking, cart, horse; the Dublin mail through Athlone and the post by horse to Roscommon; news by letter, by the fair, by word of mouth. Soldiers home from the French wars.

places.name: Kilteevan Village
places.looks: A muddy road runs between low stone walls and a handful of whitewashed cottages. Smoke lifts from the clustered roofs.
places.story: Cill Taobháin means Taobhán's church. The old people say the saint kept his cell near where the road bends.
ways: a short lane east to the whitewashed Letter Office
a rutted boreen west to Connolly Cottage

places.name: Letter Office
places.looks: A narrow counter, pigeonholes of folded paper, and a small turf fire. The room smells of sealing wax, turf smoke, and damp wool.
ways: the lane back west to the village road

places.name: Connolly Cottage
places.looks: A peat fire warms the single room. A scrubbed table, a spinning wheel by the hearth, and rain-dark coats by the door.
ways: the boreen climbing east to the village road
